Headline: Before Sugar Bay, I was a corporate lawyer. I had studied business science and law at UCT and was working at one of South Africa’s top corporate firms. On paper, I was doing what I was supposed to be doing. I just couldn’t see myself doing it for the rest of my life.  In 1999, I started thinking seriously about what kind of work I actually wanted. I loved the beach, children, water sports, teaching people new things and creating experiences. Somewhere in that process I remembered a film I had loved as a child about children meeting at a summer camp.  South Africa didn’t really have a summer camp culture at the time, so my husband Nic and I started looking at whether the idea could work here. We both resigned from our jobs and spent 14 months putting the business plan together. In 2001 we secured a bank loan and built Sugar Bay from bare land into a 100-bed camp in Zinkwazi Beach in four months.  A month after we opened, 9/11 changed a large part of the original plan. We had expected American camps travelling to South Africa to make up a significant part of the business, and those bookings disappeared almost overnight. We had to rethink things quickly and start building a market for residential camp among South African families and schools who had largely never grown up with the concept.  Twenty-five years later, Sugar Bay is still here. Some campers have returned more than 50 times. Many have come back as counselors, and some of those counselors have gone on to become managers, build careers of their own and even send another generation of children to camp.  One thing I got wrong at the beginning was how much emphasis I placed on facilities and equipment. Those things matter, but over the years I have realised that the relationships matter more. Children remember the counselor who knew their name, listened to them, encouraged them and gave them their full attention.  Running Sugar Bay has taught me a great deal about leadership, risk, responsibility, staff development and earning the trust of parents and schools year after year. What still matters most to me is seeing what camp can do for a young person. A child arrives not knowing anyone, tries something new, makes friends and goes home a little more confident and independent than when they arrived. After 25 years, that is still the best part of what we do.
